title: When the Letter Breaks
premise: In 1746, in the garrison town of Ashcombe, apprentice clockmaker Beatrix Winterbourne has spent her life mending mechanisms while keeping herself unremarkable—until the army requisitions the town for a treason trial and seizes the parish ledger that records who belongs and who does not. When the condemned are to be transported and one berth remains on the last ship, Beatrix must decide between her ailing master, her found-family of townsfolk marked as outsiders, and a stranger's child with no name in any book. She ultimately forges a new page into the ledger itself—an act of quiet, criminal justice—giving the berth to the child and staying behind to face the consequences, discovering that belonging is something you build, not something you're granted.
about_author: Coral Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish registers and shipping manifests before turning to fiction. Her novels explore the small acts of defiance recorded nowhere, and she writes from a coastal cottage full of unreliable clocks.

chapters.title: The Escapement
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Summoned to repair the observatory's master clock, she works through the night, establishing her philosophy: people are gears, history happens elsewhere, and invisibility is safety. A small kindness to a dockhand's orphaned daughter, Nell, plants the found-family seed. Emotional beat: contentment built on deliberate smallness, about to be tested.

chapters.title: Red Coats at the Door
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Soldiers occupy Ashcombe to stage a treason trial after a failed Jacobite sympathizer is betrayed. The army requisitions homes, including her master Aldous's workshop, and confiscates the parish ledger—the document deciding who are residents and who are vagrants subject to transport. Emotional beat: the sickening realization that paper can erase a life.

chapters.title: Names and Absences
chapters.summary: Alternating Beatrix and Aldous POV. They learn the ledger lists Aldous but not Beatrix, whose apprenticeship was never formally recorded—a bureaucratic ghost. Aldous's worsening cough becomes clear. Meanwhile Nell appears at the workshop, hungry; Beatrix feeds her against her own rules. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into protectiveness.

chapters.title: The Trial of Thomas Ferris
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV from the public gallery. The trial is theater; the accused, a printer she barely knew, is condemned in an afternoon. But his testimony names townsfolk who sheltered him—including half of Ashcombe's outcasts. Beatrix sees her neighbors' names being gathered like kindling. Emotional beat: outrage at justice as performance.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. He confesses he once falsified an entry to save Beatrix from the workhouse, teaching her that records can be weapons or mercies. He begins drafting a petition using his guild standing. Beatrix copies documents by candlelight, learning the clerk's hand. Emotional beat: inheritance—not of tools, but of moral craft.

chapters.title: The Reckoning List
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The army posts the transport list: thirty names to be shipped to the colonies, including Aldous, the dockhand widow, and Nell's only protector. One extra berth exists on the ship—claimed by rank, unless someone acts. Beatrix petitions the magistrate and is rebuffed with polite cruelty. Emotional beat: despair curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: A Forgery of Mercies
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Beatrix and Aldous plan to alter the ledger: expunge a dead man's entry, insert Nell under a fabricated family line, and shift Aldous's status to buy him appeal time. Each step risks hanging. The widow refuses escape, insisting her place be given to the child. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into purpose; found family choosing each other.

chapters.title: Nightwork
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Using her clockmaker's fine hands and a stolen impression of the clerk's seal, she breaks into the requisitioned records office during the blackout of the observatory clock she herself sabotaged. The forgery nearly fails when a sentry lingers; she hides among the shelves beside the very ledger. Emotional beat: the climax of nerve—stillness inside mortal danger.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At the docks, the list is read aloud. The forged entry holds; Nell is called forward as 'Winterbourne, ward.' Aldous, spared transport by the altered record, collapses coughing—and chooses to stay in Ashcombe rather than flee, telling Beatrix the town needs someone who remembers. Emotional beat: grief and triumph braided together.

chapters.title: A New Page
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, months later. The trial's fallout fades; the army withdraws. Beatrix formally enters herself and Nell into the restored ledger—truthfully this time—and takes over the workshop as Aldous declines gently toward his end. The master clock runs true again. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; belonging written in one's own hand at last.
